claim: From a beggar in the Colosseum to a convent torched near Boston.

end.title: Ursuline Convent riots
end.description: Mob violence and destruction of Catholic Convent in Boston

knots.passage: Benedict Joseph Labre spent the later years of his life within the walls of the Colosseum, living on alms, before he died in 1783.
knots.hatnote: Long after the gladiators, the ruins had at least one resident.

knots.passage: Labre's confessor, Marconi, wrote his biography and attributed 136 separate cures to his intercession within three months of his death. Those miracles were instrumental in the conversion of the Reverend John Thayer, the first American Protestant clergyman to convert to Catholicism, who was resident in Rome at the time of St. Benedict's death.
knots.hatnote: When the Colosseum beggar died, his confessor credited him with a flood of miracles.

knots.passage: Thayer was educated at Yale College and was a Protestant in his early life. He was ordained as a Congregationalist minister and served as a chaplain during the American Revolutionary War. While visiting Rome in 1783, he converted to the Roman Catholic faith, an act which caused a sensation in New England at the time.
knots.hatnote: The convert was a Boston-born, Yale-educated Revolutionary War chaplain.

knots.passage: After his death, his estate was used to found an Ursuline convent on Mount Benedict in Charlestown, Massachusetts. It was founded by the three daughters of the family with whom he lived while in Limerick. The first convent to be established in New England, it was burned down by a nativist crowd in anti-Catholic rioting in 1834.
knots.hatnote: His estate outlived him, and paid for something new in New England.

knots.passage: At about 11:00, a crowd of 50–60 men (as estimated by the Boston Evening Transcript; the Mercantile Journal estimated the crowd as between 150 and 200) set fire to tar barrels on the convent grounds. Several fire companies were called to the scene, but declined to intervene, instead joining a crowd of spectators, which eventually grew to around 2,000 people. No city in the United States at the time had a professional police force.
knots.hatnote: August 1834, after rumours of a nun held against her will.

knots.passage: The ruins of the convent remained in place for many years afterward, presenting a stark contrast to the nearby Bunker Hill Monument, completed in 1843. The property was eventually turned over to the Diocese of Boston, which sold it in 1875. Between then and the 1890s, Ploughed Hill was leveled, used to fill the nearby Middlesex Canal and marshlands along the Mystic River, and its site has since been built over with housing. Stones from the convent ruins were used to build an arch in the vestibule of the Cathedral of the Holy Cross in Boston (the cathedral church of the Archdiocese of Boston).
knots.hatnote: The burned ruins stood for decades, and then they moved.

payoff: A Colosseum beggar's miracles converted a Yale chaplain; his estate built a convent, a mob burned it, and its stones joined Boston's cathedral.
caveats: Labre's page says he lived in the Colosseum 'for a time' in his last years; the Colosseum page says he spent his later years there.
